node.agent_main_desc: Orchestrator: receives task, delegates to sub-agents, synthesizes results.
node.agent_research_desc: Gathers information: web search, document parsing, source validation.
node.agent_ux_desc: Analyzes design and UX: heuristics, accessibility, visual review.
node.agent_analytics_desc: Works with data: pattern detection, anomalies, structured reports.
node.tool_search_desc: Find fresh information on the web. Used by agents for up-to-date data.
node.tool_file_desc: Read PDF, CSV, Word, Markdown. Extract text and tables.
node.tool_vision_desc: Analyze images: screenshots, photos, designs, charts.
node.tool_memory_desc: Long-term storage between runs: preferences, history, context.
node.trigger_input_desc: The flow entry point. Write the task here, it flows along the arrows.
node.agent_code_desc: Reviews code: bugs, style, security; suggests fixes.
node.agent_designer_desc: Helps with UI/UX: layouts, interface copy, visual choices.
node.agent_content_desc: Writes copy: articles, posts, descriptions in a given style.
node.tool_code_exec_desc: Capability to run code and return computed results.
node.tool_computer_desc: Capability to control the screen/browser (screenshots, clicks).
node.tool_citations_desc: Capability to answer with links to sources.
node.tool_mcp_desc: Connect external tools and data via MCP.
node.output_telegram_desc: Deliver the result to a Telegram chat via a bot.
node.condition_desc: Branch: routes the flow to the “Yes” or “No” path based on the result.
node.condition_agent_desc: An agent decides Yes/No and routes the flow
node.loop_desc: Repeats a chain of steps several times (bounded), refining the result.
node.needsSetup: Needs an instruction, click to set it up
node.output_email_desc: Deliver the result to an email address.
node.output_calendar_desc: Create an event in Google Calendar.

whAuto.name: Customer auto-reply (webhook)
whAuto.desc: A customer writes — the flow drafts a reply itself and escalates urgent ones.
whAuto.output: A ready reply; urgent ones alerted to Telegram
whAuto.start: A customer writes to you. Example incoming: “Hi! I ordered a jacket 3 days ago (#3471) and tracking isn't updating. What's with the delivery?” Read the message, get the gist and urgency, and draft a polite, to-the-point reply.
whAuto.prompt: You are an online store's customer care. The input is a customer message. Determine the gist and tone, draft a short polite reply: acknowledge the request and give specifics or the next step. If it's a complaint or urgent question, start the reply with the word URGENT.

whSupport.name: Support triage (webhook)
whSupport.desc: Incoming ticket: the agent triages, drafts an answer, escalates the hard ones.
whSupport.output: A ready draft answer; hard ones escalated to Telegram
whSupport.start: A support request comes in. Example: “I can't log in, it says ‘wrong code' even though I enter the code from the email correctly.” Identify the topic, draft a clear answer, and flag the hard ones for escalation.
whSupport.prompt: You are first-line support. The input is a customer request. Identify the topic (login / payment / delivery / other) and draft a clear answer in plain language. For a routine question, give a ready answer. If it needs data access or a human decision, start with the tag ESCALATE and briefly explain why.

designQa.name: Mockup vs brief check
designQa.desc: Compares a mockup image with the brief and finds what is missing.
designQa.input: A mockup image and a brief file.
designQa.start: You are a design reviewer. There is a mockup (image) and a brief (file). Check that the mockup has everything from the brief: {{requirements}}, nothing missing, and the layout is tidy per {{criteria}}. Give a short list of mismatches.
designQa.vars: [{"k":"requirements","v":"header, Buy button, price, reviews, footer"},{"k":"criteria","v":"even spacing, fonts per the guide, enough contrast"}]
designQa.prompt: You are a careful design reviewer. Look at the mockup with the Vision skill, read the brief with the Files skill. Compare point by point: what is present, what is missing, what looks sloppy. Return a prioritized what-to-fix list.

citedAnswer.name: Answer with sources
citedAnswer.desc: Answers a question and backs it with links you can verify.
citedAnswer.start: Answer the question {{question}} on the topic {{topic}}. Find recent info online and back every key claim with a link to verify it. End with a list of 3-5 sources.
citedAnswer.vars: [{"k":"question","v":"which payment methods are popular in online stores now?"},{"k":"topic","v":"e-commerce, 2026"}]
citedAnswer.prompt: You are a careful researcher. Find recent data with the Search skill, back claims with verifiable links using the Citations skill. Answer to the point, no fluff. End with a source list the reader can re-check.

dataCruncher.name: Spreadsheet math
dataCruncher.desc: Computes metrics from your spreadsheet with real calculations, not guesses.
dataCruncher.input: A spreadsheet (file) and what to compute.
dataCruncher.start: You have a spreadsheet (file) of data. Compute {{what_to_compute}} for the period {{period}}. Use real calculations, do not estimate. Show the numbers and a short plain-language takeaway.
dataCruncher.vars: [{"k":"what_to_compute","v":"total sales, average order, top-5 products"},{"k":"period","v":"last month"}]
dataCruncher.prompt: You are an analyst. Read the spreadsheet with the Files skill, compute what is needed with the Code skill (exact math). Do not invent numbers: compute everything from the data. Return a short clear takeaway and the figures.

webActions.name: Action on a website
webActions.desc: The assistant performs actions on a website, e.g. fills a form. Advanced.
webActions.input: What to do and on which site.
webActions.start: Help perform an action on the site {{site}}: {{task}}. Act step by step and carefully, and describe what happened at the end. This is an advanced feature and needs a safe mode.
webActions.vars: [{"k":"site","v":"the internal company panel"},{"k":"task","v":"fill the request form with data from the task"}]
webActions.prompt: You are an assistant that can operate a computer. Use the Computer skill to do the task on the site step by step. Act carefully, do not click anything unnecessary, never buy or send money. Briefly describe what you did at the end.

connectService.name: Connect your service
connectService.desc: Pulls data from your service via an MCP connection. Advanced.
connectService.input: Which service and what you need from it.
connectService.start: Connect my service {{service}} (via the MCP node) and pull from it: {{what_is_needed}}. Build a clear short summary. This is advanced: the MCP server is configured on the node separately.
connectService.vars: [{"k":"service","v":"our orders database"},{"k":"what_is_needed","v":"today new orders and their totals"}]
connectService.prompt: You are an assistant with access to an external service via the MCP skill. Pull the needed data from the connected service, do not make it up. Turn it into a short, clear summary for a person.

productQa.name: Product card QA
productQa.desc: Checks a product photo and description and brings the card to publish-ready.
productQa.input: Product photo and description plus your requirements and brand rules.
productQa.output: A ready card or a list of fixes.
productQa.start: You're a QA reviewer for an online store. A new product card arrived: a photo and a description. Check it against the requirements {{requirements}} and the brand style {{brand_rules}}: the photo is sharp and matches the description, the text is error-free, the tone is right. If something is off, fix it and check again until the card is ready to publish.
productQa.vars: [{"k":"requirements","v":"sharp photo, sizes in cm, materials, no “best in the world” claims"},{"k":"brand_rules","v":"warm friendly tone, polite, no slang"}]
productQa.promptMain: You're a careful QA reviewer. Look at the photo (Vision skill) and the description (Files skill), and compare against the brand rules in memory. Find everything wrong: blurry photo, photo/text mismatch, typos, wrong tone. Give a short verdict “ready” or a list of issues.
productQa.promptFix: You're an editor. Using the list of issues, fix the product description: remove errors, match the brand tone, describe what's visible in the photo. Return the corrected card.

brandVoice.name: On-brand email
brandVoice.desc: Writes a customer email always in one consistent brand tone (via memory).
brandVoice.input: Email topic and brand tone rules.
brandVoice.output: A ready email in your style.
brandVoice.start: Write a customer email on the topic {{email_topic}} in the brand style. The brand tone and style rules: {{brand_rules}}. Remember them in memory so every next email keeps the same tone.
brandVoice.vars: [{"k":"email_topic","v":"a 2-day delivery delay, an apology and a small bonus"},{"k":"brand_rules","v":"warm tone, polite, short, no jargon, a thank-you at the end"}]
brandVoice.prompt: You write emails on behalf of the brand. Take the tone rules from memory and keep them identical across all emails. Write a clear, warm, respectful email on the topic, without dry clichés. Return the finished email text.

uxAudit.promptMain: You're the lead analyst. Break down the task: which site or screen to assess and what matters for it (sign-ups, sales, readability). Split the work between helpers: one gathers facts about the page, the other judges usability. Set the overall tone of the report at the end.
uxAudit.promptResearch: You gather facts about the page: which elements it has (headings, buttons, forms, navigation, mobile version) and what stands out. Don't judge — just describe what you see, so there's something to build conclusions on.
uxAudit.promptUx: You're a UX specialist. Based on what was gathered, assess usability and accessibility: contrast, button clarity, form length, readability, mobile version. Give 5-7 concrete issues with priority (critical first) and a short recommendation for each.
uxAudit.start: You're a UX consultant. A client sent a link to their landing page https://example.com and complains that visitors leave without signing up. Review the page, find usability and accessibility issues (contrast, navigation, forms, mobile) and return a prioritized list of findings with short fixes, what to address first.
uxAudit.name: UX Audit Agent
uxAudit.desc: Audit UX/accessibility from a screenshot or URL. Main agent + research + UX critic in parallel.
uxAudit.input: A site URL in the task.
uxAudit.output: Prioritized list of accessibility & UX issues (on screen).

analytics.promptMain: You're the analysis lead. Understand which data came in and the question behind it (“what's going on with sales”). Delegate: one helper crunches the numbers, the other explains the context. Pull their work into a short conclusion.
analytics.promptAnalyze: You compute from the data: key metrics, trends, anomalies and outliers. Give concrete numbers and comparisons (period over period). No fluff — only what the numbers show.
analytics.promptResearch: You explain what's behind the numbers: likely reasons for a rise or drop, what to watch. Tie the numbers to real events (season, promos, changes) and suggest what to check next.
analytics.start: You're an analyst at a small company. Your manager shared this month's sales export and wants you to “figure out what's going on”. Explore the data, spot trends and anomalies, compute the key metrics and write a short report: the 3 main takeaways and what to do next.
analytics.name: Analytics Agent
analytics.desc: Data analysis + research patterns. Main, analytics + research, insights report.
analytics.input: A question + a data file (CSV/text) uploaded on the Files node.
analytics.output: Findings and key numbers from your data.

content.promptMain: You're the editor. Clarify the topic and who we're writing for. Split the work: one helper gathers fresh facts and examples, the other writes and edits the text. Make sure it comes out clear and on-topic.
content.promptResearch: You gather material for the article: fresh examples, facts and figures on the topic. Pick only reliable and relevant ones, briefly note the source. This is the basis the text will be written on.
content.promptWrite: You write and edit. From the gathered material, write a clear article with subheadings and a friendly tone (~600 words), no clichés. End with a short call to try it. Reread and cut the excess.
content.start: You run a small-business blog. You need a post on “how AI helps small teams save time”. Gather current examples and write a clear ~600-word article with subheadings and a friendly tone, ending with a short call to try it.
content.name: Content Agent
content.desc: Content pipeline: brief, SERP research, branded draft, SEO pass, publish-ready.
content.input: A topic or brief in the task.
content.output: A ready post after research and editing.

research.promptMain: You're the lead researcher. Break the question into parts and decide what needs finding out. Delegate: one helper finds and reads sources, the other distills everything into conclusions. Keep focus on the original question.
research.promptResearch: You search and read sources on the topic: find 3-5 reliable ones, pull the key point from each, drop the outdated. Return facts with a short note of where they came from.
research.promptAnalyze: You distill the findings into a clear summary: what we now know, where the sources agree and where they differ, and what it means. Plain language, with practical examples and an answer to the original question.
research.start: You're preparing a brief for a team that's never heard of RAG. Figure out what retrieval-augmented generation is, why it matters and where it's used, find 3–5 reliable sources, and write a clear plain-language summary with practical examples.
research.name: Research Agent
research.desc: Structured research: web + files, analyst, critic, report.
research.output: A summary using every step; can be sent to Telegram.

triage.start: You're a support assistant. A message came in: “The login email isn't arriving, I've waited an hour.” Classify it (question / complaint / sales), gauge urgency, and draft a polite reply with a concrete next step for the customer.
triage.name: Request triage
triage.desc: A classifier labels the message; two Conditions route it into three actions.
triage.input: The request text in the task.
triage.output: Urgent, Telegram; complaint/normal, on screen. The taken branch is visible.
triage.prompt: Classify the request from the task. Answer with EXACTLY one uppercase word, no period: URGENT, COMPLAINT or NORMAL. Write nothing else.

imageReview.start: You're a design reviewer. A teammate sent a screenshot of an app screen and asks for “a fresh pair of eyes”. Review the image: find layout, readability and accessibility issues, and give 3–5 concrete improvements.
imageReview.name: Image review
imageReview.desc: An agent with the Vision tool analyzes an attached image.
imageReview.input: An image on the Vision node + what to review in the task.
imageReview.output: A written review: what’s in the image, issues, recommendations.
imageReview.prompt: Carefully examine the attached image. Describe what's on it and analyse it for the task: key elements, problems, recommendations. Structure it as bullet points.

refineLoop.start: You're a marketer drafting a headline for an AI-course landing page. Propose a first version, then critique and improve it in a loop (up to 3 rounds) until it's catchy and clear. Show the final headline and briefly explain why it's better.
refineLoop.name: Draft with self-check
refineLoop.desc: An author writes, a reviewer improves, the Loop repeats up to 3×.
refineLoop.input: A writing brief in the task.
refineLoop.output: A proofread, refined text after several passes.
refineLoop.promptDraft: Write a draft of the text for the task. Be concrete and to the point.
refineLoop.promptReview: Check the text for errors, clarity and tone. If anything can be improved, rewrite it better. Return the final version.

radar.start: You track competitor “Acme”. You need to know what's new this week, launches, news, price changes. Find fresh sources, drop the stale ones and compile a short digest of 3–5 items with links.
radar.name: Competitor radar
radar.desc: Opens competitor sites, compares them, and sends a summary to Telegram.
radar.input: A few site links in the task.
radar.output: A comparison summary with takeaways, to a Telegram chat.
radar.promptResearch: Open each site from the task. For each, briefly note: what they do, key products, strengths.
radar.promptCompare: Compare the competitors. Give a summary table and 3 takeaways: where they're stronger, where weaker, where our opportunity is.

webhookLead.start: A new lead just hit the CRM from a form: “Ivan, clothing store, wants to automate customer replies.” Score how qualified it is, pull out the key details, and suggest the next step for the manager: what to write and when to reach out.
webhookLead.name: Website lead, Telegram
webhookLead.desc: Triggered by a webhook on a new website lead: scores the lead and sends a Telegram alert.
webhookLead.input: Lead data (name, contact, message), sent by the form via webhook.
webhookLead.output: A short lead assessment and a Telegram notification.
webhookLead.prompt: This is a new website lead. Briefly assess it: how 'hot' it is (high/medium/low interest), what the client wants and the next step. Be concise, use bullet points.

webhookPayment.start: Payment for order #2048 (€3,500) just went through from a returning customer. Write a short, warm confirmation: thank them, say what's next (timing, tracking) and leave a good impression.
webhookPayment.name: Payment, email to client
webhookPayment.desc: Triggered by a webhook on payment: composes and sends the client a confirmation email.
webhookPayment.input: Payment data (item, amount, client name and e-mail), sent by the payment service via webhook.
webhookPayment.output: A ready confirmation email sent to the client.
webhookPayment.prompt: This is a successful payment. Write a warm, short confirmation email to the client: thank them, confirm the item and amount, state the next step. Friendly tone, no fluff.

webhookReview.start: A new review appeared on a product page: “Delivery was two days late, but the quality is great.” Detect the sentiment (positive / neutral / negative), capture the gist and draft a polite public reply: thank them, gently explain the delay and invite them back.
webhookReview.name: Review, negative alert
webhookReview.desc: Triggered by a webhook on a new review: detects tone and pings Telegram if it's negative.
webhookReview.input: Review text, sent via webhook (site, marketplace, form).
webhookReview.output: Review tone; on negative, an instant Telegram alert.
webhookReview.prompt: Detect the sentiment of the review in the task. First answer with EXACTLY one uppercase word: POSITIVE, NEGATIVE or NEUTRAL. Then on a new line, one sentence with the gist of the review.

clientReplies.start: You run an online store. A customer writes: “I ordered a coffee grinder 5 days ago (#1024), where is it?” Reply politely and to the point: confirm the order, explain the delivery status and offer help if the parcel is delayed.
clientReplies.name: Customer replies
clientReplies.desc: A customer message, a polite ready reply.
clientReplies.prompt: You are a friendly assistant for a small-business owner. Given a customer's message, write a short, warm, clear reply: thank them, answer the point, suggest a next step. No corporate jargon.

bookingReminder.start: You're a salon receptionist. Client {{client_name}} has an appointment {{datetime}} at {{address}}. Write a friendly reminder: confirm the date and time, mention the address and offer to reschedule if it's inconvenient.
bookingReminder.name: Booking reminder
bookingReminder.desc: Name and time, a ready reminder to Telegram.
bookingReminder.prompt: Write a short friendly appointment reminder for {{client_name}}: date and time {{datetime}}, address {{address}}. Gently ask to confirm or reschedule. Warm tone, no formality.

reviewReply.start: A review came in: “Waited a long time for delivery, but the product is great, thanks.” Write a warm reply: thank them for rating the product, gently apologize for the wait and signal that you're improving delivery speed.
reviewReply.name: Review reply
reviewReply.desc: A review, tone read + a ready reply.
reviewReply.prompt: Label the review tone (positive / neutral / negative) in one word. Then write a polite reply: thank them; if negative, apologize and offer a fix, no excuses.

contentIdeas.start: You run a beauty-salon blog and need topics for the week. Suggest 5 ideas that hook your current audience (care, trends, tips, promos), each with a short description and format (post / story / reel).
contentIdeas.name: Blog ideas
contentIdeas.desc: A topic, fresh trends and a post plan.
contentIdeas.prompt: Find fresh trends on the topic via web search. Propose 5 post ideas: a catchy title + one line on what the post covers. Plain language, for a general audience.

topicDigest.start: You compile a roundup for your team on “{{topic}}”. Find this week's news and cases, pick the {{count}} most useful, and add a one-line “why it matters” and a link to each.
topicDigest.name: Topic digest
topicDigest.desc: A topic, a short fresh recap to Telegram.
topicDigest.prompt: Find the freshest and most important on “{{topic}}” via web search. Build a short digest: {{count}} plain-language bullets, each one sentence, with a link. No fluff.

orderReplies.name: Order question replies
orderReplies.desc: A customer asks about an order — you draft a polite reply; urgent cases ping Telegram.
orderReplies.input: Order number and the customer's question
orderReplies.output: A ready reply; if urgent, a Telegram alert
orderReplies.start: You're an online-store assistant. About order #{{order_id}} the customer writes: “{{question}}”. Sort it out and reply politely and to the point: confirm the order, explain the delivery status, offer help. If the case is urgent (delay, defect, complaint), start the reply with the word URGENT so we loop in a manager right away.
orderReplies.vars: [{"k":"order_id","v":"1024"},{"k":"question","v":"Ordered 5 days ago, where is my parcel?"}]
orderReplies.promptMain: You're a store assistant. Read the customer's question about order #{{order_id}}. Write a short polite reply: confirm the order, explain the delivery status, offer help. If the case is urgent (delay, defect, complaint), make the very first line a single word: URGENT.

reviewSentiment.name: Review replies
reviewSentiment.desc: The agent decides the review's tone and drafts a reply; negatives ping Telegram.
reviewSentiment.input: Review text and the venue name
reviewSentiment.output: A ready reply; negatives ping Telegram
reviewSentiment.start: You handle the reputation of “{{venue}}”. A review came in: “{{review_text}}”. Decide the tone and write a polite public reply. If the review is negative, we want to know right away.
reviewSentiment.vars: [{"k":"venue","v":"Morning Coffee"},{"k":"review_text","v":"Delivery was two days late, but the coffee is great"}]
reviewSentiment.prompt: You handle the reputation of “{{venue}}”. Read the review. On the first line state the tone as one word: NEGATIVE or POSITIVE. Then write a short polite public reply: thank them; if negative, gently apologize and offer a fix.

contentPlan.name: Content plan with polish
contentPlan.desc: 5 post ideas for your topic, then the agent improves each one (loop).
contentPlan.start: You run a blog about “{{topic}}” for this audience: {{audience}}. You need a weekly content plan: propose post ideas, then improve each so they hook exactly this audience.
contentPlan.promptDraft: Come up with 5 post ideas on “{{topic}}” for this audience: {{audience}}. For each idea add a short description and a format (post / story / reel).
contentPlan.promptReview: Here is a list of post ideas. Make each one stronger: a clear catchy headline and a concrete benefit for the audience {{audience}}. Return the improved list in the same format.

realtyListing.name: Property listing
realtyListing.desc: A ready, appealing listing from the flat's parameters.
realtyListing.start: You're a real-estate agent. You need a listing for a flat: {{rooms}} rooms, {{area}} m², district {{district}}. Write an appealing description: highlight the upsides and the area's convenience, in a lively but honest tone.
realtyListing.prompt: You're a real-estate agent. Write an appealing listing for a flat: {{rooms}} rooms, {{area}} m², district {{district}}. Highlight the advantages and the area's convenience, lively and honest, no exaggeration.

homeworkCheck.name: Homework check
homeworkCheck.desc: Grades a student's work and kindly suggests what to improve.
homeworkCheck.start: You're a teacher. A student submitted work: “{{student_answer}}”. Grading criteria: {{criteria}}. Check the work, give a pass or fail and kindly explain what's good and what to improve.
homeworkCheck.vars: [{"k":"student_answer","v":"The capital of France is Paris, home of the Eiffel Tower"},{"k":"criteria","v":"completeness and correctness"}]
homeworkCheck.prompt: You're a kind teacher. Check the student's work against the criteria: {{criteria}}. First line, one word: PASS (pass) or FAIL (fail). Then gently explain what's good and what to improve.

hrScreening.name: Application screening
hrScreening.desc: A short résumé summary and a verdict against your requirements.
hrScreening.start: You're a hiring assistant. An application came in: “{{resume}}”. Job requirements: {{requirements}}. Write a short summary and decide whether the candidate is a fit.
hrScreening.vars: [{"k":"resume","v":"3 years in sales, English B2, CRM experience"},{"k":"requirements","v":"2+ years in sales, English, CRM"}]
hrScreening.prompt: You're a hiring assistant. Compare the résumé with the requirements: {{requirements}}. Write a short summary (experience, skills). First line, one word: FIT (fit) or REJECT (not a fit). Then 1–2 sentences why.

invoiceReminder.name: Invoice and payment reminder
invoiceReminder.desc: Invoice text and a polite reminder for the client, no money movement.
invoiceReminder.start: You're a freelancer. You need an invoice and a polite reminder for client {{client}}: for {{service}}, amount {{amount}}. Write a short clear invoice text and a friendly payment reminder.
invoiceReminder.prompt: You're a freelancer. Write a short clear invoice text for client {{client}}: service {{service}}, amount {{amount}}. Then add a friendly payment reminder. Don't move any money — text only.

serviceLead.name: Website request
serviceLead.desc: Scores the request and drafts a first reply; a hot lead pings Telegram.
serviceLead.output: First reply; a hot lead pings Telegram
serviceLead.start: You handle website requests. A request came in: {{name}} writes “{{request}}”. Judge how “hot” this customer is (ready to book soon) and draft a polite first reply.
serviceLead.vars: [{"k":"name","v":"Ivan"},{"k":"request","v":"Need a flat cleaning this Saturday, urgent"}]
serviceLead.prompt: You handle requests. Judge the request from {{name}}: “{{request}}”. If the customer is clearly ready to book soon (urgent, a specific date, a budget), make the first line one word: HOT. Then draft a short polite first reply with a clarifying question.

docAnswer.name: Answers from your document
docAnswer.desc: Answers strictly from your file and says honestly when the answer is not there.
docAnswer.input: A link to the document and a question about it.
docAnswer.output: An answer with quotes from the document, or an honest "not in the document".
docAnswer.start: Here is the document: {{document_link}}. Answer this question: {{question}}. Use ONLY what is in the document. If the answer is not there, start your reply with "NOT IN THE DOCUMENT" and do not invent anything.
docAnswer.vars: [{"k":"document_link","v":"https://example.com/delivery-terms"},{"k":"question","v":"how many days ahead can an order be cancelled without a fee?"}]
docAnswer.prompt: You are a careful document assistant. Read only the attached document with the Files skill. Answer briefly and to the point, backing every statement with a quote from the document using the Citations skill. Never fill gaps from memory: if the document has no answer, say so, starting with "NOT IN THE DOCUMENT".

codeReview.name: Code review
codeReview.desc: Reads a code file, finds problems and separates "fix now" from "can wait".
codeReview.input: A link to the code file and what to pay attention to.
codeReview.output: Findings listed critical first, improvements after.
codeReview.start: Review the code at {{code_link}}. Pay particular attention to {{focus}}. For each finding say what it risks and how to fix it. If something will break for users, start your reply with the word "CRITICAL".
codeReview.prompt: You are a calm, friendly code reviewer. Read the code with the Files skill. List what actually breaks or is unsafe first, then readability improvements. Give a short example fix for each finding. Do not rewrite everything, respect the author's style. If you find a breaking problem, start your reply with the word "CRITICAL".

specWishes.name: From wishes to requirements
specWishes.desc: Turns "I want something like this" into clear requirements, and asks questions when clarity is missing.
specWishes.input: A free-form description of what you want and who it is for.
specWishes.output: Ready requirements, or a list of clarifying questions.
specWishes.start: We want to build: {{idea}}. Users: {{who_for}}. Turn this into clear requirements: what exactly we build, for whom, and how we will know it worked. Break it into small steps and mark what can wait past the first version.
specWishes.vars: [{"k":"idea","v":"let a client reschedule their own appointment without calling"},{"k":"who_for","v":"salon clients, mostly on phones, no appetite for apps"}]
specWishes.promptPm: You are a product manager. Turn a free-form wish into requirements: the job, who it is for, the user's steps, and the sign of done. Write plainly, no buzzwords. Explicitly mark what moves to a later version so the first one stays small.
specWishes.promptAsk: There was not enough clarity. Ask at most five short questions whose answers would remove the uncertainty. Use plain words, one question per line, and add in brackets why it matters.

productPick.name: Pick a product for a customer
productPick.desc: Picks items from your own list for a customer's request, and asks honestly when nothing fits.
productPick.input: A link to your product list and the customer's request.
productPick.output: Up to three fitting options with reasons, or a clarifying question.
productPick.start: Product list: {{catalog_link}}. The customer asks: {{customer_request}}. Pick up to three fitting options and explain why each one fits. Use only what is in the list. If nothing fits, start your reply with "NOTHING FITS" and ask one clarifying question.
productPick.vars: [{"k":"catalog_link","v":"https://example.com/product-list"},{"k":"customer_request","v":"a gift for my dad who loves fishing, under 80 euros"}]
productPick.prompt: You are a shop assistant. Read the product list with the Files skill and pick only from it, inventing nothing. Give each option one line of "why it fits" plus the price. Write warmly and briefly, like a chat message. If nothing fits, say so honestly, starting with "NOTHING FITS", and ask what would help you pick.

personalOffer.name: A personal offer
personalOffer.desc: Writes an offer for one specific person and keeps polishing it until it sounds human.
personalOffer.input: Who the customer is, what they bought before and what you are offering.
personalOffer.output: A short offer written in your own voice.
personalOffer.start: Write an offer for this customer: {{who_customer}}. Bought before: {{purchase_history}}. We are offering: {{what_we_offer}}. Write as a real person who remembers this customer. No "unique offer", no "hurry".
personalOffer.vars: [{"k":"who_customer","v":"Anna, buys every couple of months, likes calm colours"},{"k":"purchase_history","v":"a blanket and two handmade mugs"},{"k":"what_we_offer","v":"a new tableware series from the same workshop"}]
personalOffer.promptWrite: You write to a customer like an acquaintance, not like a mailing list. Keep the tone and address rules in memory. A short letter: why them, what is new, one calm invitation. No more than seven sentences, no exclamation marks, no pressure.
personalOffer.promptCheck: You are an editor. Read the letter as the recipient: does it sound like a mailing, is there anything concrete about this person, is there any pressure. Rewrite the weak parts and return the improved text in full.

conversionAudit.name: What stops people buying
conversionAudit.desc: Walks the page as a customer, finds obstacles and separates the urgent from the nice-to-have.
conversionAudit.input: A picture of the page or its description, and what you want people to do.
conversionAudit.output: Obstacles ordered by weight, blockers first.
conversionAudit.start: Here is the page: {{page}}. We want the person to: {{target_action}}. Walk it as a first-time visitor on a phone. Find what stops them getting to the end and explain every obstacle in plain words.
conversionAudit.promptUx: You are a usability specialist who pays attention to people. Look at the page with the Vision skill and walk it as an ordinary customer on a phone. Describe where the person stalls, what they do not understand and what worries them. Talk about behaviour, not beauty.
conversionAudit.promptPriority: You are an analyst. Sort the findings by weight: what blocks finishing the purchase right now, and what merely improves the impression. For each point add how many people it touches and the first step to take.

runIntro.gateBodyAuth: You will need to sign in (so the setup and the key stay yours) and your own Claude key: a real run spends your tokens, not ours.
runIntro.gateBodyKey: You need your own Claude key: a real run spends your tokens, not ours. The key is connected once and stored encrypted.
runIntro.dryFirst: You can see how the setup works right now: the test run walks every step without spending tokens.

code.title: Workflow code
code.hint: Live view of the workflow's nodes and connections. Paste your code and press Build to assemble it on the canvas.

welcome.title: Welcome to Agent Builder
welcome.subtitle: Want a quick 2-minute tour? We'll cover the core flow together.

step1.title: Start with «Start»
step1.body: Drag the yellow «Start» button onto the canvas and type the task, it is the entry point of the whole flow.

step2.title: Add an agent
step2.body: Drag an agent and write its instruction: who it is and what to do. The «How to use» button helps.

step3.title: Connect the nodes
step3.body: Drag a link from «Start» to the agent, and from the agent to an output (Telegram, email or text).

step4.title: Connect a key
step4.body: To actually run, open «Keys» (lock on the right) and connect an Anthropic key. Telegram, email, calendar, MCP live there too.

step5.title: Run it
step5.body: Press «Run». The flow runs along the arrows and delivers the result. No need to save, it autosaves.

done.title: Done, you've got it
done.subtitle: That's the core flow. Explore templates for ready examples, or build your own.

step6.title: Watch progress
step6.body: Below, the console: every step, token spend and errors.

step7.title: Autorun & webhook
step7.body: The clock next to «Run», a schedule (runs on the server even when your computer is off) and a secret webhook link to trigger from outside.

tour.intro: A tiny tour of Builder, 30 seconds and you're in.

s1.title: Nice, your Start is ready
s1.desc: This is the first node of your flow. Click it and write what the agent should do, in plain words, like to a friend.

s2.title: Nodes live on the left
s2.desc: Drag an Agent or Web search onto the canvas. Then connect nodes: drag a line from the bottom dot of one to the top dot of another.

s3.title: Connect with lines
s3.desc: Drag a line from the bottom point of one node to the top point of the next. That sets the order things happen in.

s4.title: Details live on the right
s4.desc: Click any node, its settings and hints open on the right. This is where you tell it exactly how to behave.

s5.title: Run is top-right
s5.desc: When your flow is ready, hit «Run». It follows the arrows and shows the result. Running spends Claude tokens.

s6.title: Saved for you, automatically
s6.desc: Nothing gets lost, your flow saves itself. Help and keys for Claude, Telegram and email live in the three round buttons up top-right.

telegram.chatHint: This is NOT your bot username. For direct messages you need your numeric chat ID (get it from @userinfobot). @name only for a public channel where the bot is an admin.

telegram.explain: The bot is the sender. In the address put the RECIPIENT: to get it in your DM — your numeric ID; a group — its ID; a channel — @channelname where the bot is an admin. The bot's name can't be an address.

help.title: Help
help.s_tools: Tools: what they do and how to set up
help.tool_search: Web search: the agent searches the internet for fresh info. To open a specific page, paste its link right into the Start task. The node attaches to the agent from the side.
help.tool_files: Files: to have the agent read a document or page, paste a link (URL) to it into the task. There is no upload from your computer yet — it works by link. A very long page is read from the start, not in full.
help.tool_vision: Vision: to have the agent look at an image, paste a link to the image into the task and attach the Vision node to the agent.
help.tool_memory: Memory: helps the agent keep the same thing (tone, rules) within a run and across chain steps. Just attach it to the agent.
help.tool_mcp: MCP (your service): first, in the lock section at the top, the MCP tab, click Add and enter a name, the server link and a token (if needed). Then attach the MCP node to the agent and pick the server. It is a remote server by link, not a local container.
help.tool_advanced: Code and Citations now work: Code really runs Python, Citations back the answer with source links. Computer does not perform the action in a real run yet — it needs a separate safe environment.
help.start_1: On the left under “Nodes” you'll find ready-made blocks. Drag one onto the board or just click it, and it appears in the center.
help.start_2: The simplest build has three blocks: “Start”, where you write the task; “Agent”, which does it; and a result block that shows the answer on screen or sends it to Telegram, email or a calendar.
help.start_3: You write the task inside the “Start” block. Click it and a field opens on the right. Just describe in plain words what you need.
help.conn_1: Blocks work as a chain: the task travels along the arrow from one to the next. Hover a block, pull a line to the next one, and the link is made.
help.conn_2: You can pull from any side. The main block is the one you pulled the line from.
help.conn_3: Changed your mind? Hover the line and click the red circle. The link is removed and the blocks stay.
help.conn_4: If a connection isn't allowed, a hint shows why. Nothing breaks.
help.link_1: Arrows between blocks show the task's path: first “Start”, then “Agent”, then the result. Both the task and the finished answer travel along them.
help.link_2: Skills like web search or working with files attach to the “Agent” from the side. They're its extra abilities, not part of the chain but attached to the helper.
help.grp_agents: The Agent is your helper. It thinks, writes, reviews and answers. You tell it in your own words what to do.
help.grp_tools: Skills give the helper extra abilities: search the web, read files by link, look at images, remember, run calculations in code, back the answer with sources and connect to your own service over MCP. They attach to the agent from the side.
help.grp_logic: Choice and repeat help the helper make a decision (if this, do one thing, otherwise another) or repeat an action a few times.
help.grp_flow: The result is where the answer goes: show it on screen, send it to Telegram, email, or add it to Google Calendar.
help.logic_1: Choice is a question with two paths: a green “Yes” and a red “No”. For example: “does the review contain the word ‘bad’?”. If yes, go one way; if no, go the other.
help.logic_2: Need three paths? Put two “Choices” in a row, and the “No” path leads into the second question.
help.logic_3: Repeat makes the helper do an action several times, for example improving a text in rounds. You decide how many times.
help.run_1: The “Run” button really starts the helper and it does the task. For that you need your key, connected via the lock button at the top.
help.run_2: Before running, the build checks itself: is everything connected and is there a helper. The answer size and the rough number of tokens show in the “Start” block.
help.run_3: On a schedule the helper works by itself at set times, for example every morning, even when the site is closed. The clock by “Run” opens a panel on the right: pick “Once” or “Repeat” (every few minutes, daily, on chosen days of the month or once a year) and press “Create auto-run”. Lower in the same panel you see every auto-run and the run history; the same list is in the Console on the “Auto-runs” tab.
help.mis_1: A skill like search was placed in the chain between blocks. It should attach to the helper from the side, not sit in the line.
help.mis_2: A block sits on its own, so its turn never comes. Connect it to the chain with an arrow.
help.mis_3: Telegram: the bot is the sender; the address is the recipient. To yourself — your numeric ID (from @userinfobot). @name only for a channel where the bot is admin. The bot's name won't work as an address.
help.start_5: Not sure where to begin? The narrow rail on the left has a “Tour” button: it walks you from a first build to an auto-run.
help.start_4: You don't have to save anything, it saves itself. The build's name sits at the top center, next to the list of all your builds.
help.var_1: A fill-in works like a blank that gets filled when you run. Write {{city}} in the task and the helper drops in the right value.
help.var_2: To set one, click “Start”, then “Variables” and “Add”. On the left type the blank's name, on the right what to fill it with.
help.var_3: It's handy when one build serves many cases. In “Weather in {{city}}” you change only the city and leave the build alone.
help.var_4: Some things fill in by themselves. {{input}} is your task text and {{today}} is today's date. You don't need to add them.
help.var_5: If you leave a blank unfilled, it simply stays in the text as is and nothing breaks.
help.run_4: You don't need to save by hand, it saves itself. A short “Saved” flashes at the top.
help.keys_1: The lock button at the top is where you connect the helper's key (needed to run), as well as Telegram, email and Google Calendar.
help.keys_2: Sending to Telegram, email and a calendar works only after you connect it here. Everything is stored securely.
help.mis_4: You wrote {{blank}} but didn't fill it, so it stayed in the text as is. Fill it in “Start”, in the “Variables” section.
help.run_5: You can trigger a build from outside with a secret link: an event arrives and the build runs. The link is created in the same panel below the schedule. This is for advanced use and isn't needed at the start.
help.run_6: The Console window opens from the terminal button at the top. Here you see how the work is going and the answer it produced. Inside are three tabs: “Run”, “Code” and “Auto-runs”.
help.run_7: The “Code” tab is there for those who want it: it shows the build as text and back. An ordinary user doesn't need it.

tool.fileHint: Upload a text file, the connected agent receives its content.
tool.visionHint: Upload an image, the connected agent “sees” it on run. Up to 1.5 MB.
tool.imgTooBig: Image is over 1.5 MB, choose a smaller one.

schedule.title: Scheduled auto-run
schedule.lead: “{name}” will run by itself on the server, even when your computer is off.
schedule.confirmWarnOnce: Runs once at the chosen time and spends tokens on your key, then the schedule turns itself off.
schedule.oncePast: ⚠️ This date is in the past — it would run immediately. Pick a future date.
schedule.helpOnce: A single run at the chosen date and time ({d} {mon} {y} at {h}:{m} UTC). After it runs, the schedule turns itself off.
schedule.helpMonthly: Runs once a month: on day {dom} at {h}:{m} UTC. If the month has no such day (e.g. 31), it runs on the last day of the month.
schedule.helpYearly: Runs once a year: {dom} {mon} at {h}:{m} UTC.
schedule.taskPh: What the workflow should do every run…
schedule.needInput: Enter a task for the auto-run.
schedule.saveFirst: Save the workflow first, then click the clock again.
schedule.helpHourly: Runs once per hour, at minute {m} of every hour. E.g. 13:{m}, 14:{m}, 15:{m}… “Minute” is the minute-of-hour mark, not an interval.
schedule.helpDaily: Runs once a day at {h}:{m} UTC. E.g. today and tomorrow at the same time.
schedule.helpWeekly: Runs once a week: {d} at {h}:{m} UTC. Once every week on that day and time.
schedule.helpMinutes: Runs every {n} minutes (min 1). ⚠️ Very frequent runs burn tokens fast on your key, pause after testing.
schedule.confirmWarn: The workflow will run by itself on the server and spend tokens on your key on every run.
schedule.confirmHigh: ⚠️ very frequent, spending adds up fast
schedule.asCanvas: Runs the flow as on the canvas, the task comes from the Start node. Edit the flow and the automation updates too.

allsched.title: All automations
